title: Born too late, Stan Getz and turning down Count Basie
summary: He has few regrets, mentions Getz's offer, and regrets turning down Basie's band.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: Do you think if you could be born at a different time — did you ever feel like you were born a little too late?
Since I’m now still alive, no. Because I would have been long gone.

But guys have told me that jeez if you were around in the 40’s and like that, like you’d be — Stan Getz offered me a gig that night at Carnegie Hall, right after the gig. We went up to the party afterwards because we did this thing and he played with the band, and he said when you get off this band call me. I never did. But I understand that he was not the most fun guy to work with.
Well I’m jealous of some of your playing experiences, because I often times think I was born a little too late. But we’re both still here. And I’m going to remember that answer.

Yeah because I’d be gone, long gone. But man I can’t say that I have an awful lot of regrets in life. I mean my life ambition in high school was to someday play with Woody Herman’s band and Maynard Ferguson’s band. And I had achieved both of that when I was 27. So I mean I was offered Count Basie’s band, when I was with Maynard’s band, and I said — I was offered that twice I think and I turned it — I am kind of regretful that I turned it down. Although I do have a feeling that the intensity that I was playing and the style that I was playing and accustomed to playing with Maynard’s band, I might not have been — it would have taken some adjusting to go with Basie’s band, you know, because we were on top of everything. We were playing way on top of the beat and with Basie it was much more laid back. And probably Basie might have had to have a talk with me if I had taken the job.
